works.title: NeurIPS 2025 Foundation Models Meet Embodied Agents Challenge: Systems, Analysis, and Lessons Learned
works.summary: While Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated impressive high-level reasoning capabilities, their deployment in embodied decision-making tasks remains hindered by a lack of standardized, diagnostic evaluations. We present a retrospective on the NeurIPS 2025 Embodied Agent Interface Challenge, which systematically benchmarked LLMs across four critical reasoning modules: goal interpretation, subgoal decomposition, action sequencing, and transition modeling. Hosted on the BEHAVIOR and VirtualHome simulators, the competition departed from traditional, binary task-success metrics. Instead, it leveraged Linear Temporal Logic (LTL) to evaluate alternative viable trajectories and introduced fine-grained metrics to pinpoint specific failures, such as affordance violations, hallucinations, and missing preconditions. The competition attracted significant engagement globally, with 58 registered teams developing diverse solutions. An analysis of the winning and most innovative submissions reveals a clear trend: while hybrid neuro-symbolic pipelines and test-time compute significantly enhance trajectory feasibility, spatial relationship modeling remains a pervasive bottleneck for current LLMs. In this report, we detail the competition design, summarize the top-performing methodologies, and present key lessons learned to guide the future development of robust, interpretable embodied AI systems.

works.title: Counterfactual World Models: JEPAs That Reason About "What If"
works.summary: World models operate in a world they cannot fully observe. When a hidden disturbance, such as a current pushing a boat, changes the outcome of an action, a counterfactual question follows: what would have happened under a different action, subject to the same disturbance? Its answer separates bad decisions from bad luck. We prove that world models trained on factual transitions cannot answer it on their own, whatever their data or capacity. For many physical systems, the observed outcome and a simple property of the dynamics suffice: natura non facit saltus, nature makes no leaps. When actions and disturbances act as separate forces, their interaction is second-order in time, so the counterfactual outcome is, to first order, the observed outcome plus the difference between the world model's predictions under the alternative and factual actions. This yields a counterfactual world model with no counterfactual data, extra parameters, or retraining. For transitions of duration $h$, we prove an $O(h^2)$ bound on the counterfactual error relative to the disturbance variance, establish a matching minimax lower bound from unpaired factual data, and characterize failures at discontinuities, coordinate folds, and disturbances that scale the command. We validate these predictions from pixels with JEPA world models on frozen DINOv2 and masked autoencoder (MAE) encoders. On four rendered simulators, our approach improves counterfactual $R^2$ from $38$--$46\%$ to $86$--$96\%$ with the same world models; on a fifth, an underwater vehicle, it reaches $90$--$94\%$ with sixteen times more factual data. Four further frozen encoders, DINOv3, SigLIP~2, CLIP and EVA-02, give $81$--$95\%$ on the same simulators. In hindsight planning, it finds the action that would have reached the goal in $35$--$69\%$ of events, against $14$--$23\%$ for an oracle planner that knows the simulator but not the outcome.

works.title: The Content–Geometry Tradeoff in World Models: When JEPA Learns Latent Maps
works.summary: A latent world model for planning needs two properties: latent distances that smoothly track progress toward a goal (geometry), and task-relevant factors that remain decodable from the latent representation (content). Common approaches prevent representation collapse with a stop-gradient (SG) target or a distributional regularizer, but we find that both often yield poor latent geometry. In this paper, we introduce sliced variance regularization (SVReg), which imposes a variance floor on latent projections along random directions. SVReg learns a smooth map of the agent's state. Its latent trajectories are smooth, and its latent distances track progress in navigation and reaching. These geometric benefits, however, can come with a tradeoff in content. SVReg can discard slowly changing, hard-to-predict factors, such as the pose of a manipulated object, that SG variants tend to preserve. To address this tradeoff, we propose Slow SVReg, which favors slowly changing factors with a slowness term and a gated residual predictor. It keeps these factors and improves planning. This simple recipe has the highest planning success in the hard settings of five visual control tasks, and it learns latent maps from first-person mazes and city walks.

works.title: Mapping the AI Supply Chain: Dependencies, Vulnerabilities, and Market Concentration in the AI Ecosystem
works.summary: AI systems are built across many organizations that contribute models, data, compute, capital, talent, and other assets. While the layers of the AI stack are relatively well understood, the relationships between actors and components across layers remains sparsely documented. In this work, we focus on the organizations that make up the AI supply chain: the complex network of actors that contribute to the development and deployment of AI. We motivate the examination of the organizational AI supply chain---highlighting concerns about concentration, power, chokepoints, cascading failures, fragmented accountability, and risk---then describe our pipeline for mapping the AI supply chain. Our pipeline yields our main contribution: a multilayered, large-scale dataset of actors and relationships in the AI ecosystem, annotated with dates, descriptions, types, tags, and more. This work takes a step toward systematically mapping and measuring the AI supply chain and its properties, cataloging how models, data, chips, infrastructure, capital, and even talent flow between organizations. This data enable critical examinations of industry relationships and yield insights into the political economy of AI development and concentration. We provide several illustrative analyses, including studying the most central actors, analyzing network concentration, and identifying communities and chokepoints. While our dataset is fairly comprehensive, it is also necessarily incomplete: public documents omit private deals, and coverage is shaped by search design. Together, the approach, data, and findings aim to serve as a resource for studying the AI ecosystem. The dataset is publicly available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/sarahcen/ai-supply-chain and can be explored interactively at https://aisupplychains.org/.

works.title: Ambient LLMs: Data-Efficient Supervised Fine-tuning via Temperature Matching
works.summary: Collecting large-scale, diverse, and high-quality post-training datasets for autoregressive language models is challenging. Consequently, Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) is typically applied to datasets significantly smaller than those used for pre-training, which leads to overfitting and the catastrophic forgetting of the tails of the data distribution. To prevent this collapse, we introduce Ambient SFT, a principled framework for leveraging imperfect predictions to augment the fine-tuning set. In our method, a "frozen" version of the pre-trained model serves as a noisy teacher that the fine-tuned model must match at a coarse level. In particular, we require that the high-temperature versions of the conditional distributions produced by the post-training model should match the high-temperature versions of the pre-training ones. The temperature hyperparameter controls the level of trust in the pre-trained model, with the limit $T\to \infty$ reverting back to regular SFT and $T=1$ to knowledge distillation. We demonstrate that our approach outperforms standard SFT across domain adaptation, instruction-tuning, and reasoning, leading for up to $21\%$ average relative improvement to standard SFT.
